back: A deterministic, lossless map text -> ids -> text: $\mathrm{dec}(\mathrm{enc}(b))=b$.

front: Character-level vs word-level vs subword tokenisation
back: Characters: tiny vocabulary, very long sequences. Words: short sequences but a huge vocabulary and unknown words. Subwords: a compromise with a tunable vocabulary and no unknowns.
Start from bytes; count adjacent pairs; merge the most frequent into a new token; record the rule; repeat for K steps.

front: Why does merging the most frequent pair compress the most?
back: A pair seen c times (non-overlapping) turns 2c tokens into c tokens, saving exactly c tokens.

front: How is new text encoded with learned merges?
back: From its bytes, repeatedly apply the present pair with the lowest rule number until no present pair is a rule.

front: How is a BPE token sequence decoded?
back: Expand each id to its bytes (merged ids are the concatenation of their two parts), join the bytes, decode as UTF-8.

front: Vocabulary size formula for byte-level BPE
back: $V = 256 + K + |\text{special tokens}|$ with K the number of merges.
The base vocabulary contains all 256 bytes, so any input can be encoded; no unknown token is needed.
Reserved ids for structure (end of text, padding, chat role markers). Matched before BPE and never split or merged.
Embedding and output tables grow as $V\cdot d$ each (unless tied), and rare tokens are poorly trained.
Fewer tokens per text: shorter sequences, cheaper attention, more text per context window, fewer generation steps.
A regex splits text into chunks (words with their leading space, numbers, punctuation) before BPE so merges do not cross word boundaries.

front: Why do non-English languages often cost more tokens?
back: A vocabulary trained mostly on English has few merges for other scripts, so their text splits into many small pieces.

front: Inputs and targets for next-token training
back: Targets are the inputs shifted by one: x = ids[:, :-1], y = ids[:, 1:], shapes (B, T) each.
